questions.q: A black body is the standard object used to study the radiation emitted by hot objects at different temperatures. What is its defining property?
options: It absorbs all incoming radiation that falls on it
It absorbs all radiation but emits none of it back
It reflects all radiation of every wavelength
It only emits radiation in the visible part of the spectrum
questions.explanation: The textbook defines a black body simply as one that absorbs all incoming radiation. Because all objects emit radiation slightly differently, scientists use this standard absorber to study the radiation emitted at different temperatures and then extrapolate. The trap option — absorbs everything but emits nothing — is wrong: a hot black body glows brightly.

questions.q: To model a black body, a very small hole is drilled through the wall of an induction furnace. Why does radiation that enters the hole make it behave as a near-perfect absorber?
options: The hole is coated in a special black paint that absorbs light
Radiation entering the hole bounces around inside the furnace cavity until the walls absorb it, so almost none escapes back out
The small hole reflects all radiation straight back out at the same wavelength
The furnace walls are transparent, letting radiation pass straight through
questions.explanation: Radiation entering the small hole is forced to bounce around in the furnace cavity until the walls absorb it, so essentially none escapes back through the hole. The radiation that does leave the hole is characteristic only of the equilibrium temperature of the cavity, not of the wall material — which is why the black body is such a useful standard.

questions.q: As the temperature of a black body increases, how does its curve of intensity versus wavelength change?
options: The peak in intensity moves to a longer wavelength and the whole curve drops lower
The peak in intensity moves to a lower (shorter) wavelength and the curve rises to a higher intensity at every wavelength
The curve stays the same shape but shifts only to longer wavelengths
The intensity increases only at long wavelengths while the peak stays fixed
questions.explanation: With increasing temperature the peak in intensity moves to a lower (shorter) wavelength, and the emission becomes more intense at every wavelength so the whole curve sits higher. Hotter objects therefore appear both brighter and bluer — the two changes the syllabus wants you to read off the curves.

questions.q: What did the classical wave theory of light predict for the intensity of black body radiation as the wavelength becomes shorter — the prediction that became known as the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'?
options: The intensity would fall smoothly to zero at short wavelengths
The intensity would peak and then decline, matching experiment
The intensity would increase without limit, approaching infinity at short ultraviolet wavelengths, which violates conservation of energy
The intensity would stay constant across all wavelengths
questions.explanation: Classical wave theory predicted that as the wavelength becomes shorter the radiation intensity would increase without limit, approaching infinity in the ultraviolet. This violates the principle of conservation of energy and contradicts the experimental curve, which has a definite peak and then declines. That short-wavelength disaster is the ultraviolet catastrophe.

questions.q: Wien's law relates the wavelength of maximum intensity, \(\lambda_{\max}\), to the absolute temperature \(T\) of a black body. Which statement is correct?
options: \(\lambda_{\max} = b\,T\), so a hotter body has a longer peak wavelength
\(\lambda_{\max} = b/T\) with \(\lambda_{\max}T\) constant at \(2.9\times10^{-3}\) K m, and \(T\) must be in kelvin
\(\lambda_{\max} = T/b\), and temperature may be in degrees Celsius
\(\lambda_{\max}\) depends on what the body is made of, not its temperature
questions.explanation: Wien's law asserts \(\lambda_{\max} = b/T\), or equivalently \(\lambda_{\max}T = \text{constant} = 2.9\times10^{-3}\) K m. The wavelength of maximum intensity depends only on the temperature of the body, which must be stated in kelvin — so the hotter the body, the shorter its peak wavelength.

questions.q: From memory: what revolutionary assumption did Max Planck make about the energy exchanged between the particles of a black body and the radiation field, and how is one packet described?
keyPoints: Planck assumed the radiant energy is exchanged not continuously but as if in multiples of a small 'lump', or quantum.
Each quantum of energy is described by E = hf, where f is the frequency and h is Planck's constant (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
This quantisation explained the experimental curve and removed the ultraviolet catastrophe, marking the birth of quantum theory.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that energy is exchanged in discrete lumps (quanta) of size hf rather than continuously, and linked it to resolving the ultraviolet catastrophe, grade yourself Good or Easy. Planck himself thought it was just a mathematical trick.

questions.q: A hotplate has a glow that is dark red. The wavelength of the most intense light it emits is 4.0 μm. Use Wien's law to find the surface temperature of the hotplate in kelvin.
questions.explanation: Rearrange Wien's law for temperature: \(T = b/\lambda_{\max}\). Substituting the textbook's values gives 725 K. The dark-red glow is consistent with a relatively cool surface and a long peak wavelength.

questions.q: The Sun has a surface temperature of approximately 5800 K. Determine the wavelength of the most intense light emitted from its surface, and state the colour seen by humans.
working: 500 nm is green-yellow, in the middle of the visible spectrum.
questions.explanation: Wien's law gives the Sun's peak wavelength as about 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (500 nm), green-yellow light near the centre of the visible band — no accident, since our eyes are most sensitive where the Sun emits most strongly.

questions.q: From memory: using the thermal-equilibrium argument, explain why a perfect absorber (a black body) must also be a perfect emitter.
keyPoints: An object at a steady temperature must radiate energy at the same rate it absorbs it, by conservation of energy.
A black body absorbs the maximum possible radiation at every wavelength.
To keep its temperature constant it must therefore emit the maximum possible at every wavelength — otherwise it would heat up without limit. So a perfect absorber is necessarily a perfect emitter.
questions.explanation: The mark is the equilibrium argument: maximum absorption forces maximum emission, or the energy books don't balance. A good absorber is a good emitter; a perfect absorber is a perfect emitter — never 'emits nothing'.

questions.q: Explain how Planck's hypothesis of quantised energy resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe. (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Classical wave theory predicted that a black body's emitted intensity should increase without limit as wavelength decreases, reaching infinity at short ultraviolet wavelengths. This contradicted the experimental curve, which peaks and then falls, and violated conservation of energy, since infinite emission is impossible. Planck proposed that the oscillating charges in the black body can only emit or absorb energy in discrete quanta, each equal to Planck's constant times the frequency (E = hf), rather than continuously. Because high-frequency, short-wavelength radiation requires large quanta, and at a given temperature such large quanta are only rarely available, high-frequency emission is strongly suppressed rather than infinite. The resulting predicted curve rises, peaks and falls in agreement with experiment, removing the ultraviolet catastrophe and marking the birth of quantum theory.

criteria.descriptor: States the classical prediction of intensity rising without limit (to infinity) at short ultraviolet wavelengths.
Identifies that this contradicts the experimental peak-and-fall curve and violates conservation of energy.
States Planck's quantisation: energy emitted/absorbed only in discrete quanta of size E = hf.
Explains the mechanism: large high-frequency quanta are rarely available, so short-wavelength emission is suppressed.
Concludes the corrected curve rises, peaks and falls in agreement with experiment.

questions.explanation: The marks live in the mechanism: state the classical infinity prediction, name the contradiction (experiment + conservation of energy), introduce quantisation with E = hf, then explain the suppression of rare high-frequency quanta. Weak answers say 'Planck quantised energy and fixed it' without the suppression step.
